source: Warmest climes but nurse the cruellest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of ceaseless verdure. Skies the most effulgent but basket the deadliest thunders: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is, that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner encounters the direst of all storms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst from out that cloudless sky, like an exploding bomb upon a dazed and sleepy town.

Towards evening of that day, the Pequod was torn of her canvas, and bare-poled was left to fight a Typhoon which had struck her directly ahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the thunder, and blazed with the lightning, that showed the disabled masts fluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the tempest had left for its after sport.

Holding by a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck; at every flash of the lightning glancing aloft, to see what additional disaster might have befallen the intricate hamper there; while Stubb and Flask were directing the men in the higher hoisting and firmer lashing of the boats. But all their pains seemed naught. Though lifted to the very top of the cranes, the windward quarter boat (Ahab’s) did not escape. A great rolling sea, dashing high up against the reeling ship’s high teetering side, stove in the boat’s bottom at the stern, and left it again, all dripping through like a sieve.

“Bad work, bad work! Mr. Starbuck,” said Stubb, regarding the wreck, “but the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can’t fight it. You see, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps, all round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me, all the start I have to meet it, is just across the deck here. But never mind; it’s all in fun: so the old song says;”—(sings.)

Oh! jolly is the gale, And a joker is the whale, A’ flourishin’ his tail,— Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh! The scud all a flyin’, That’s his flip only foamin’; When he stirs in the spicin’,— Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh! Thunder splits the ships, But he only smacks his lips, A tastin’ of this flip,— Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
“Avast Stubb,” cried Starbuck, “let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if thou art a brave man thou wilt hold thy peace.”

“But I am not a brave man; never said I was a brave man; I am a coward; and I sing to keep up my spirits. And I tell you what it is, Mr. Starbuck, there’s no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut my throat. And when that’s done, ten to one I sing ye the doxology for a wind-up.”
“Madman! look through my eyes if thou hast none of thine own.”
“What! how can you see better of a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?”

“Here!” cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder, and pointing his hand towards the weather bow, “markest thou not that the gale comes from the eastward, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? the very course he swung to this day noon? now mark his boat there; where is that stove? In the stern-sheets, man; where he is wont to stand—his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard, and sing away, if thou must!
“I don’t half understand ye: what’s in the wind?”

“Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket,” soliloquized Starbuck suddenly, heedless of Stubb’s question. “The gale that now hammers at us to stave us, we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us towards home. Yonder, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward—I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning.”
At that moment in one of the intervals of profound darkness, following the flashes, a voice was heard at his side; and almost at the same instant a volley of thunder peals rolled overhead.
“Who’s there?”
“Old Thunder!” said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain to him by elbowed lances of fire.

Now, as the lightning rod to a spire on shore is intended to carry off the perilous fluid into the soil; so the kindred rod which at sea some ships carry to each mast, is intended to conduct it into the water. But as this conductor must descend to considerable depth, that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and as moreover, if kept constantly towing there, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering not a little with some of the rigging, and more or less impeding the vessel’s way in the water; because of all this, the lower parts of a ship’s lightning-rods are not always overboard; but are generally made in long slender links, so as to be the more readily hauled up into the chains outside, or thrown down into the sea, as occasion may require.

“The rods! the rods!” cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly admonished to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been darting flambeaux, to light Ahab to his post. “Are they overboard? drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!”

“Avast!” cried Ahab; “let’s have fair play here, though we be the weaker side. Yet I’ll contribute to raise rods on the Himmalehs and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but out on privileges! Let them be, sir.”
“Look aloft!” cried Starbuck. “The corpusants! the corpusants!”

All the yard-arms were tipped with a pallid fire; and touched at each tri-pointed lightning-rod-end with three tapering white flames, each of the three tall masts was silently burning in that sulphurous air, like three gigantic wax tapers before an altar.

“Blast the boat! let it go!” cried Stubb at this instant, as a swashing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand, as he was passing a lashing. “Blast it!”—but slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone he cried—“The corpusants have mercy on us all!”

To sailors, oaths are household words; they will swear in the trance of the calm, and in the teeth of the tempest; they will imprecate curses from the topsail-yard-arms, when most they teeter over to a seething sea; but in all my voyagings, seldom have I heard a common oath when God’s burning finger has been laid on the ship; when His “Mene, Mene, Tekel Upharsin” has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pallidness was burning aloft, few words were heard from the enchanted crew; who in one thick cluster stood on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence, like a far away constellation of stars. Relieved against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet negro, Daggoo, loomed up to thrice his real stature, and seemed the black cloud from which the thunder had come. The parted mouth of Tashtego revealed his shark-white teeth, which strangely gleamed as if they too had been tipped by corpusants; while lit up by the preternatural light, Queequeg’s tattooing burned like Satanic blue flames on his body.

The tableau all waned at last with the pallidness aloft; and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two passed, when Starbuck, going forward, pushed against some one. It was Stubb. “What thinkest thou now, man; I heard thy cry; it was not the same in the song.”

“No, no, it wasn’t; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces?—have they no bowels for a laugh? And look ye, Mr. Starbuck—but it’s too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock a’ block with sperm-oil, d’ye see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three spermaceti candles—that’s the good promise we saw.”

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb’s face slowly beginning to glimmer into sight. Glancing upwards, he cried: “See! see!” and once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled supernaturalness in their pallor.
“The corpusants have mercy on us all,” cried Stubb, again.

At the base of the mainmast, full beneath the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee was kneeling in Ahab’s front, but with his head bowed away from him; while near by, from the arched and overhanging rigging, where they had just been engaged securing a spar, a number of the seamen, arrested by the glare, now cohered together, and hung pendulous, like a knot of numbed wasps from a drooping, orchard twig. In various enchanted attitudes, like the standing, or stepping, or running skeletons in Herculaneum, others remained rooted to the deck; but all their eyes upcast.

“Aye, aye, men!” cried Ahab. “Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame but lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I would fain feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it; blood against fire! So.”

Then turning—the last link held fast in his left hand, he put his foot upon the Parsee; and with fixed upward eye, and high-flung right arm, he stood erect before the lofty tri-pointed trinity of flames.

“Oh! thou clear spirit of clear fire, whom on these seas I as Persian once did worship, till in the sacramental act so burned by thee, that to this hour I bear the scar; I now know thee, thou clear spirit, and I now know that thy right worship is defiance. To neither love nor reverence wilt thou be kind; and e’en for hate thou canst but kill; and all are killed. No fearless fool now fronts thee. I own thy speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though but a point at best; whencesoe’er I came; wheresoe’er I go; yet while I earthly live, the queenly personality lives in me, and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in thy lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss thee; but at thy highest, come as mere supernal power; and though thou launchest navies of full-freighted worlds, there’s that in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, thou clear spirit, of thy fire thou madest me, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to thee.”
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames leap lengthwise to thrice their previous height; Ahab, with the rest, closes his eyes, his right hand pressed hard upon them.]

“I own thy speechless, placeless power; said I not so? Nor was it wrung from me; nor do I now drop these links. Thou canst blind; but I can then grope. Thou canst consume; but I can then be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; mine eye-balls ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems as beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Yet blindfold, yet will I talk to thee. Light though thou be, thou leapest out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of thee! The javelins cease; open eyes; see, or not? There burn the flames! Oh, thou magnanimous! now I do glory in my genealogy. But thou art but my fiery father; my sweet mother, I know not. Oh, cruel! what hast thou done with her? There lies my puzzle; but thine is greater. Thou knowest not how came ye, hence callest thyself unbegotten; certainly knowest not thy beginning, hence callest thyself unbegun. I know that of me, which thou knowest not of thyself, oh, thou omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond thee, thou clear spirit, to whom all thy eternity is but time, all thy creativeness mechanical. Through thee, thy flaming self, my scorched eyes do dimly see it. Oh, thou foundling fire, thou hermit immemorial, thou too hast thy incommunicable riddle, thy unparticipated grief. Here again with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with thee; I burn with thee; would fain be welded with thee; defyingly I worship thee!”
“The boat! the boat!” cried Starbuck, “look at thy boat, old man!”

Ahab’s harpoon, the one forged at Perth’s fire, remained firmly lashed in its conspicuous crotch, so that it projected beyond his whale-boat’s bow; but the sea that had stove its bottom had caused the loose leather sheath to drop off; and from the keen steel barb there now came a levelled flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent’s tongue, Starbuck grasped Ahab by the arm—“God, God is against thee, old man; forbear! ’tis an ill voyage! ill begun, ill continued; let me square the yards, while we may, old man, and make a fair wind of it homewards, to go on a better voyage than this.”

Overhearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew instantly ran to the braces—though not a sail was left aloft. For the moment all the aghast mate’s thoughts seemed theirs; they raised a half mutinous cry. But dashing the rattling lightning links to the deck, and snatching the burning harpoon, Ahab waved it like a torch among them; swearing to transfix with it the first sailor that but cast loose a rope’s end. Petrified by his aspect, and still more shrinking from the fiery dart that he held, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab again spoke:—

“All your oaths to hunt the White Whale are as binding as mine; and heart, soul, and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And that ye may know to what tune this heart beats; look ye here; thus I blow out the last fear!” And with one blast of his breath he extinguished the flame.

But as for me, all the start I have to meet it is just across the deck here. But never mind; it's all in fun, so the old song says —" (Sings.)
Oh! jolly is the gale, / And a joker is the whale, / A-flourishing his tail — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
The scud all a-flying, / That's his flip only foaming; / When he stirs in the spicing — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
Thunder splits the ships, / But he only smacks his lips, / A-tasting of this flip — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
"Enough, Stubb," cried Starbuck, "let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if you are a brave man you will hold your peace."

"But I'm not a brave man; I never said I was a brave man; I'm a coward, and I sing to keep my spirits up. And I'll tell you how it is, Mr. Starbuck: the only way to stop my singing in this world is to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I'll sing you the doxology to wind up with."
"Madman! Look through my eyes if you have none of your own."
"What! How can you see better on a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"

"Here!" cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder and pointing his hand toward the weather bow. "Don't you see that the gale comes from the east, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? The very course he swung to at noon today? Now look at his boat there; where is it stove? In the stern-sheets, man, where he always stands — his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard and sing away, if you must!"
"I don't half understand you; what's in the wind?"

"Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," mused Starbuck suddenly, paying no attention to Stubb's question. "This gale that now hammers at us to stave us in — we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us toward home. Over there, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward — I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
Just then, in one of the spells of deep darkness that followed the flashes, a voice was heard beside him, and almost at the same moment a volley of thunderclaps rolled overhead.
"Who's there?"
"Old Thunder!" said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain by angled lances of fire.

Now, just as the lightning rod on a spire ashore is meant to carry the dangerous fluid off into the soil, so the similar rod that some ships at sea carry to each mast is meant to conduct it into the water. But this conductor must reach down to a considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and, moreover, if it were kept towing there all the time, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering more than a little with some of the rigging and more or less slowing the vessel's way through the water. Because of all this, the lower parts of a ship's lightning-rods are not always overboard; they are generally made in long slender links, so that they can more readily be hauled up into the chains (the ledges outside the hull where the shrouds are fastened), or thrown down into the sea, as occasion requires.

"The rods! The rods!" cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly warned to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been darting like torches to light Ahab to his post. "Are they overboard? Drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!"

"Stop!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we are the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himalayas and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but away with privileges! Let them be, sir."
"Look aloft!" cried Starbuck. "The corpusants! The corpusants!"

The tips of all the yardarms were lit with a pale fire — the corpusants, or St. Elmo's fire. Each of the three tall masts, touched at every three-pronged end of its lightning-rod with three tapering white flames, burned silently in that sulfurous air like three gigantic wax candles before an altar.

"Blast the boat! Let it go!" cried Stubb at this instant, as a washing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand as he was passing a lashing. "Blast it!" But slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone, he cried: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

To sailors, oaths are everyday words; they will swear in the trance of the calm and in the teeth of the tempest; they will hurl curses from the topsail-yard-arms when most they teeter over a seething sea; but in all my voyaging, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship — when His Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — the writing on Belshazzar's wall — has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pale fire burned aloft, the spellbound crew said little. They stood in one thick cluster on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence like a distant constellation of stars. Outlined against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet-black negro, Daggoo, loomed up to three times his real height and seemed to be the black cloud the thunder had come from. Tashtego's parted lips showed his shark-white teeth, which gleamed strangely as if they too had been tipped with corpusants; and, lit up by the unnatural light, Queequeg's tattoos burned on his body like Satanic blue flames.

At last the whole scene faded along with the pale fire aloft, and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two went by; then Starbuck, going forward, bumped into someone. It was Stubb. "What do you think now, man? I heard your cry; it wasn't the same as in the song."

"No, no, it wasn't; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces? Have they no sympathy for a laugh? And look, Mr. Starbuck — but it's too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock-full of sperm-oil, d'you see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three sperm candles — that's the good promise we saw."

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into view. Glancing upward, he cried: "See! See!" And once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled otherworldliness in their pallor.
"The corpusants have mercy on us all," cried Stubb again.

At the foot of the mainmast, right under the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee knelt in front of Ahab, but with his head bowed away from him. Close by, a number of seamen who had just been securing a spar up in the arched, overhanging rigging were caught and held by the glare; they now huddled together and hung there like a cluster of numbed wasps from a drooping orchard twig. Others stood rooted to the deck in various spellbound poses, like the standing, stepping or running skeletons at Herculaneum; but every eye was turned upward.

"Aye, aye, men!" cried Ahab. "Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame only lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I want to feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it — blood against fire! So."

Then, turning — with the last link still gripped in his left hand — he set his foot on the Parsee, and with his eyes fixed upward and his right arm flung high, he stood upright before the towering three-pronged trinity of flames.

"Oh! You clear spirit of clear fire, whom I once worshipped on these seas as a Persian, until in the sacramental act I was so burned by you that to this hour I bear the scar — I know you now, you clear spirit, and I know now that the right way to worship you is defiance. You will be kind to neither love nor reverence; and even for hate you can only kill; and all are killed. It is no fearless fool who faces you now. I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life I will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though only a point at best — wherever I came from, wherever I go — yet while I live on earth, the queenly personality lives in me and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in your lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss you; but at your highest, come as mere supernal power, and though you launch navies of fully laden worlds, there is something in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, you clear spirit, you made me out of your fire, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to you."
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames shoot up lengthwise to three times their former height; Ahab, like the rest, shuts his eyes, pressing his right hand hard over them.]

"I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; didn't I say so? Nor was it wrung out of me; nor do I drop these links now. You can blind; but then I can grope. You can consume; but then I can be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; my eyeballs ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Blindfolded, I will still talk to you. Light though you are, you leap out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of you! The javelins stop; open, eyes; do you see, or not? There burn the flames! Oh, you magnanimous one! Now I do glory in my genealogy. But you are only my fiery father; my sweet mother I do not know. Oh, cruel! What have you done with her? There lies my puzzle; but yours is greater. You do not know how you came to be, and so you call yourself unbegotten; you certainly do not know your beginning, and so you call yourself unbegun. I know something of myself that you do not know of yourself, oh you omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond you, you clear spirit, to whom all your eternity is only time, all your creativeness mechanical. Through you, your flaming self, my scorched eyes dimly see it. Oh, you foundling fire, you hermit immemorial, you too have your incommunicable riddle, your unshared grief. Here again, with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! Leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with you; I burn with you; I long to be welded with you; defiantly I worship you!"
"The boat! The boat!" cried Starbuck, "look at your boat, old man!"

Ahab's harpoon, the one forged in Perth's fire, was still lashed firmly in its conspicuous crotch, so that it stuck out beyond the bow of his whaleboat. But the sea that had stove in the boat's bottom had knocked off the loose leather sheath, and from the sharp steel barb there now streamed a level flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent's tongue, Starbuck seized Ahab by the arm. "God, God is against you, old man; hold back! This is an evil voyage! Badly begun, badly continued. Let me square the yards while we still can, old man, and make a fair wind of it for home, and go on a better voyage than this."

Hearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew ran to the braces at once — though not a single sail was left aloft. For the moment they seemed to share all the horrified mate's thoughts, and they raised a half-mutinous shout. But Ahab flung the rattling lightning links down on the deck, snatched up the burning harpoon, and waved it among them like a torch, swearing he would run it through the first sailor who so much as cast loose a rope's end. Petrified by his look, and shrinking still more from the fiery dart in his hand, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab spoke again:

"Every oath you swore to hunt the White Whale binds you as tightly as mine binds me; and heart, soul and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And so that you may know what tune this heart beats to — look here: this is how I blow out the last fear!" And with a single blast of breath he put out the flame.

As in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men flee the neighborhood of some lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength only make it all the more unsafe, because all the more a target for thunderbolts; so at those last words of Ahab's, many of the sailors did run from him in a terror of dismay.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 119 — Lysene
paragraphs: Det er de varmeste himmelstrøg, der nærer de grusomste tænder: tigeren i Bengalen ligger på lur i krydrede lunde med aldrig visnende grønt. Det er de mest blændende himle, der bærer de dødeligste tordenvejr i deres kurv: det pragtfulde Cuba kender tornadoer, som aldrig har fejet over tamme nordlige lande. Således er det også, at søfareren i disse strålende japanske have møder den mest frygtelige af alle storme, tyfonen. Den kan undertiden bryde ud af en skyfri himmel som en bombe, der eksploderer over en omtåget og søvnig by.

Hen mod aften den dag fik Pequod sit sejldug revet af og blev, med bare master, overladt til at kæmpe mod en tyfon, der havde ramt hende lige forfra. Da mørket faldt på, brølede og revnede himmel og hav af torden og blussede af lyn, der viste de ødelagte master, hvor pjalter her og der flagrede, som stormens første raseri havde efterladt dem til sin efterleg.

Med en hånd om et vant stod Starbuck på agterdækket og kastede ved hvert lyn et blik op i det indviklede rigning for at se, hvilken yderligere ulykke der kunne være sket der, mens Stubb og Flask ledede mandskabet i at hejse bådene højere op og surre dem fastere. Men alle deres anstrengelser syntes forgæves. Selv om den var hejst helt op til kranernes top, slap agterbåden i luv (Ahabs) ikke. En stor rullende sø, der slog højt op mod det vaklende skibs høje, svajende side, slog bunden ind på båden i agterenden og forlod den igen, dryppende igennem som en si.

»Dårligt arbejde, dårligt arbejde, Mr. Starbuck,« sagde Stubb og så på vraget, »men havet må have sin vilje. Stubb for sit vedkommende kan ikke kæmpe imod det. Ser du, Mr. Starbuck, en bølge har sådan et stort langt tilløb, før den springer — helt rundt om jorden løber den, og så kommer springet! Men hvad mig angår, så er alt det tilløb, jeg har til at møde den, kun hen over dækket her. Men lad det være; det er det hele for sjov, som den gamle vise siger —« (Synger.)
Åh! Glad er stormen, / og en spøgefugl er hvalen, / når den svinger med sin hale — / sikke en morsom, sportslig, spilfærdig, spøgefuld, sjov og løjerlig knægt, havet er, åh!
Skumsprøjtet, det flyver, / det er kun hans flip, der skummer; / når han rører i krydderiet — / sikke en morsom, sportslig, spilfærdig, spøgefuld, sjov og løjerlig knægt, havet er, åh!
Torden splitter skibe, / men han smasker kun med læberne, / mens han smager på denne flip — / sikke en morsom, sportslig, spilfærdig, spøgefuld, sjov og løjerlig knægt, havet er, åh!
»Nok, Stubb,« råbte Starbuck, »lad tyfonen synge og slå sin harpe her i vores rigning; men hvis du er en modig mand, holder du mund.«

»Men jeg er ikke en modig mand; jeg har aldrig sagt, at jeg var en modig mand; jeg er en kujon, og jeg synger for at holde modet oppe. Og jeg skal sige dig, hvordan det er, Mr. Starbuck: den eneste måde at få mig til at holde op med at synge i denne verden er at skære halsen over på mig. Og når det er gjort, er der ti mod en på, at jeg synger dig doksologien til slut.«
»Gale mand! Se gennem mine øjne, hvis du ingen har selv.«
»Hvad! Hvordan kan du se bedre end andre på en mørk nat, uanset hvor tåbeligt det er?«

»Her!« råbte Starbuck, greb Stubb i skulderen og pegede med hånden mod luvbovgen. »Ser du ikke, at stormen kommer fra øst, netop den kurs, Ahab skal sejle mod Moby Dick? Den kurs, han svingede ind på ved middagstid i dag? Se nu på hans båd derovre; hvor er den slået itu? I agterrummet, mand, hvor han altid står — hans standpunkt er slået itu, mand! Hop nu over bord og syng løs, hvis du absolut skal!«
»Jeg forstår dig kun halvt; hvad er der i vente?«

»Ja, ja, rundt om Kap det Gode Håb er den korteste vej til Nantucket,« mumlede Starbuck pludselig uden at give agt på Stubbs spørgsmål. »Denne storm, der nu hamrer løs på os for at slå os itu — den kan vi vende til en gunstig vind, der driver os hjemad. Derovre, i luv, er alt dommens sorthed; men i læ, hjemad — jeg ser det lysne op der; men ikke af lynet.«
I netop det øjeblik, i en af de dybe mørkeperioder, der fulgte efter lynene, hørtes en stemme ved siden af ham, og næsten i samme øjeblik rullede en byge af tordenskrald hen over deres hoveder.
»Hvem der?«
»Gamle Torden!« sagde Ahab, mens han famlede sig frem langs skansekledningen til sit drejehul; men så pludselig fik sin vej oplyst af kantede lanser af ild.

Nu, ligesom lynlederen på et spir i land er beregnet på at føre det farlige fluidum ned i jorden, således er den lignende stang, som nogle skibe til søs fører på hver mast, beregnet på at lede det ned i vandet. Men denne leder må række ned til en betydelig dybde, så dens ende undgår enhver berøring med skroget; og desuden ville den, hvis den hele tiden blev slæbt efter skibet, være udsat for mange uheld, foruden at den ville genere noget af rigningen en del og mere eller mindre sinke skibets gang gennem vandet. På grund af alt dette ligger de nedre dele af et skibs lynledere ikke altid udenbords; de er som regel lavet af lange, smalle led, så de lettere kan hales op i rusterne (de afsatser uden på skroget, hvor vantene er fæstnet) eller kastes ned i havet, alt efter behov.

»Lynlederne! Lynlederne!« råbte Starbuck til mandskabet, pludselig vækket til årvågenhed af det skarpe lyn, der netop havde fløjet som fakler for at lyse Ahab til hans plads. »Er de udenbords? Smid dem over, for og agter. Hurtigt!«

»Stop!« råbte Ahab; »lad os have fair play her, selv om vi er den svageste side. Dog vil jeg bidrage til at sætte lynledere op på Himalaya og Andesbjergene, så hele verden kan være sikret; men væk med særrettigheder! Lad dem være, hr.«
»Se op!« råbte Starbuck. »Korpusanterne! Korpusanterne!«

Spidserne af alle rær var tændt af en bleg ild — korpusanterne, eller sankt Elms ild. Hver af de tre høje master, rørt ved hver trekløftet ende af sin lynleder af tre spidse hvide flammer, brændte lydløst i den svovlagtige luft som tre kæmpestore vokslys foran et alter.

»Pokker tage båden! Lad den gå!« råbte Stubb i det øjeblik, da en skyllende sø løftede sig under hans egen lille båd, så dens essing voldsomt klemte hans hånd, mens han slog en surring. »Pokker tage den!« Men han gled baglæns på dækket, og hans opadvendte øjne fangede flammerne; og straks skiftede han tone og råbte: »Korpusanterne forbarme sig over os alle!«

For sømænd er eder hverdagsord; de vil bande i dødvandets trance og lige i stormens kæft; de vil kaste forbandelser ned fra mærsrånokker, når de mest vipper over et kogende hav; men på alle mine rejser har jeg sjældent hørt en almindelig ed, når Guds brændende finger har været lagt på skibet — når hans Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — skriften på Belsasars væg — er blevet vævet ind i vanterne og tovværket.

Mens denne bleke ild brændte oppe i toppen, sagde den fortryllede besætning kun lidt. De stod i én tæt klump på back, og alle deres øjne glimtede i det bleke fosforlys som et fjernt stjernebillede. Aftegnet mod det spøgelsesagtige lys tårnede den kæmpestore kulsorte mand Daggoo sig op til tre gange sin virkelige højde og syntes at være den sorte sky, som tordenen var kommet fra. Tashtegos adskilte læber viste hans hajhvide tænder, som glimtede underligt, som om også de var tippet med korpusanter; og oplyst af det unaturlige lys brændte Queequegs tatoveringer på hans krop som sataniske blå flammer.

Til sidst forsvandt hele synet sammen med den blege ild oppe i riggen, og endnu en gang var Pequod og hver eneste sjæl på hendes dæk svøbt i et ligklæde. Der gik et øjeblik eller to. Så stødte Starbuck, der var på vej forover, ind i nogen. Det var Stubb. »Hvad siger du nu, mand? Jeg hørte dit råb. Det lød ikke som i sangen.«

»Nej, nej, det gjorde det ikke. Jeg sagde, at korpusanterne har barmhjertighed med os alle, og det håber jeg stadig, de har. Men har de kun barmhjertighed med lange ansigter? Har de ingen medfølelse med et grin? Og se, Mr. Starbuck — men det er for mørkt til at se. Hør så her: jeg tager den flamme, vi så på mastetoppen, som et tegn på held. For de master står plantet i et lastrum, der snart bliver stuvende fuldt af spermolie, ser du. Og så vil al den sperm stige op i masterne som saft i et træ. Ja, vores tre master bliver endnu som tre spermlys — det var det gode løfte, vi så.«

I det øjeblik fik Starbuck øje på Stubbs ansigt, der langsomt begyndte at skimte frem af mørket. Han så opad og råbte: »Se! Se!« Og endnu en gang kunne man se de høje, spidse flammer, og deres bleghed virkede nu, som om den var fordoblet i uhyggelighed.
»Korpusanterne har barmhjertighed med os alle,« råbte Stubb igen.

Ved foden af stormasten, lige under doblonen og flammen, knælede parseren foran Ahab, men med hovedet bøjet væk fra ham. Tæt ved var en flok sømænd, som netop havde været oppe at surre en rå i den buede, overhængende rigning, blevet grebet og holdt fast af skæret. Nu sad de sammen og hang der som en klynge følelsesløse hvepse på en nedhængende kvist i en frugthave. Andre stod som naglet til dækket i alle slags fortryllede stillinger, som de stående, gående eller løbende skeletter i Herculaneum. Men hvert eneste øje var vendt opad.

»Ja, ja, mænd!« råbte Ahab. »Se op på den. Læg godt mærke til den. Den hvide flamme lyser kun vejen til den hvide hval! Ræk mig de lænker fra stormasten dér. Jeg vil mærke denne puls og lade min slå mod den — blod mod ild! Sådan.«

Så vendte han sig — med den sidste lænke stadig i sin venstre hånd — satte foden på parseren, og med blikket rettet opad og højre arm kastet højt rejste han sig op foran den tårnhøje, trespidsede treenighed af flammer.

»Åh! Du klare ånd af klar ild, som jeg engang tilbad på disse have som perser, indtil jeg i den hellige handling blev så brændt af dig, at jeg endnu i dag bærer arret — jeg kender dig nu, du klare ånd, og jeg ved nu, at den rette måde at tilbede dig på er trods. Du vil ikke være venlig mod hverken kærlighed eller ærbødighed. Og selv for had kan du kun dræbe, og alle bliver dræbt. Det er ingen uforfærdet tåbe, der står over for dig nu. Jeg anerkender din ordløse, stedløse magt. Men til sidste åndedrag i mit jordskælvsliv vil jeg bestride dens ubetingede, ufuldstændige herredømme over mig. Midt i det personliggjorte upersonlige står her en personlighed. Selv om den i bedste fald kun er et punkt — uanset hvor jeg kom fra, og hvor jeg skal hen — så lever den dronningelige personlighed, så længe jeg lever på jorden, i mig og føler sine kongelige rettigheder. Men krig er smerte, og had er jammer. Kom i din laveste form som kærlighed, og jeg vil knæle og kysse dig. Men i din højeste form, kom som ren overjordisk magt, og selv om du sender flåder af fuldt lastede verdener af sted, er der noget herinde, der stadig forbliver ligeglad. Åh, du klare ånd, du skabte mig af din ild, og som et sandt ildens barn ånder jeg den tilbage til dig.«
[Pludselige, gentagne lyn. De ni flammer skyder på langs op til tre gange deres tidligere højde. Ahab lukker, ligesom de andre, øjnene og presser sin højre hånd hårdt mod dem.]

»Jeg anerkender din ordløse, stedløse magt. Sagde jeg det ikke? Den blev heller ikke vristet ud af mig, og jeg slipper ikke disse lænker nu. Du kan blinde, men så kan jeg famle. Du kan fortære, men så kan jeg være aske. Tag imod disse stakkels øjnes og lukkehænders hyldest. Jeg ville ikke tage imod den. Lynet farer gennem min kranie. Mine øjeæbler gør ondt og gør ondt. Hele min slagne hjerne virker halshugget og trillende hen over en bedøvende grund. Åh, åh! Med bind for øjnene vil jeg stadig tale til dig. Lys er du, men du springer ud af mørke. Men jeg er mørke, der springer ud af lys, springer ud af dig! Spyddene holder inde. Åbn jer, øjne. Ser I, eller ser I ikke? Dér brænder flammerne! Åh, du storsindede! Nu er jeg virkelig stolt af min slægt. Men du er kun min ildfader. Min søde moder kender jeg ikke. Åh, grusomme! Hvad har du gjort med hende? Dér ligger mit mysterium, men dit er større. Du ved ikke, hvordan du blev til, og kalder dig derfor ufødt. Du kender helt sikkert ikke din begyndelse, og kalder dig derfor ubegyndt. Jeg ved noget om mig selv, som du ikke ved om dig selv, du almægtige. Der er noget uudstrålende hinsides dig, du klare ånd, for hvem hele din evighed kun er tid og hele din skaberkraft mekanisk. Gennem dig, dit flammende selv, ser mine svedne øjne det svagt. Åh, du hittebarnsild, du ældgamle eneboer, også du har din uudtalelige gåde, din usagte sorg. Her læser jeg igen, i hovmodig kval, min fader. Spring! Spring op og slik himlen! Jeg springer med dig. Jeg brænder med dig. Jeg længes efter at blive smeltet sammen med dig. Trodsigt tilbeder jeg dig!«
»Båden! Båden!« råbte Starbuck. »Se på din båd, gamle mand!«

Ahabs harpun, den der var smedet i Perths ild, sad stadig fast surret i sin iøjnefaldende gaffel, så den stak ud over forstavnen på hans hvalbåd. Men havet, der havde slået hul i bådens bund, havde slået den løse læderskede af, og fra den skarpe stålbarb strømmede nu en vandret flamme af bleg, kløvet ild. Mens den tavse harpun brændte dér som en slanges tunge, greb Starbuck Ahab i armen. »Gud, Gud er imod dig, gamle mand. Hold igen! Det er en ond rejse! Dårligt begyndt, dårligt fortsat. Lad mig brasse rårne, mens vi endnu kan, gamle mand, og lave en god vind af den til hjemturen og sejle en bedre rejse end denne.«

Da den rædselsslagne besætning hørte Starbuck, løb den straks hen til brasserne — selv om der ikke var et eneste sejl tilbage oppe. Et øjeblik syntes de at dele alle den forfærdede styrmands tanker, og de udstødte et halvt mytterisk råb. Men Ahab slyngede de rasslende lynlænker ned på dækket, rev den brændende harpun op og svingede den blandt dem som en fakkel. Han svor, at han ville støde den gennem den første sømand, der så meget som slap en tovende løs. Forstenede af hans blik og endnu mere skræmte af den flammende pil i hans hånd veg mændene forfærdede tilbage, og Ahab talte igen:

»Hver ed, I svor på at jage den hvide hval, binder jer lige så fast, som min binder mig. Og med hjerte, sjæl og krop, lunger og liv er gamle Ahab bundet. Og for at I kan vide, hvilken melodi dette hjerte slår efter — se her: sådan blæser jeg den sidste frygt ud!« Og med ét pust slukkede han flammen.

Som mænd i den orkan, der fejer hen over sletten, flygter fra nærheden af et ensomt, kæmpemæssigt elmetræ, hvis netop højde og styrke gør det så meget mere usikkert, fordi det så meget mere er et mål for tordenkiler, således løb ved disse sidste ord fra Ahab mange af sømændene væk fra ham i skræk og forfærdelse.
